butir.teks: The fourth is the scrupulousness (wara') of the truthful ones (siddiqin): turning away from everything other than Allah Most High, out of fear of spending an hour of one's life on what does not add any nearness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, even if one knows and is certain that it does not lead to anything forbidden. All these degrees lie outside the jurist's concern except the first degree, which is the scrupulousness of witnesses and of judgeship and of what impugns probity; and doing that does not remove sin in the Hereafter. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said to Wabisa, "Seek a ruling from your heart, even if they give you a ruling, even if they give you a ruling." (٢) The jurist does not speak about the pangs of hearts and how to act on them, but only about what impugns probity, because all of the jurist's concern is tied to this world, through which the path of the Hereafter is set right. If he does speak about something of the qualities of the heart and the rulings of the Hereafter, that enters his speech incidentally, just as something of medicine, arithmetic, astronomy, and theology (kalam) enters his speech, and as wisdom enters grammar and poetry.

Sufyan ath-Thawri, who was an imam in outward knowledge, used to say, "Seeking this is not part of the provision for the Hereafter." How could it be, when they agree that the nobility of knowledge lies in acting on it? How, then, can it be thought that it is the knowledge of zihar, li'an, salam, ijara, and sarf? Whoever learns these matters in order to draw near to Allah Most High through them is mad. Rather, the action is of the heart and the limbs in acts of obedience, and nobility lies in those actions. If you say, "Why did you put jurisprudence on the same level as medicine, when medicine too relates to this world, namely the health of the body, and the soundness of religion is also connected with it? And this equating contradicts the consensus of the Muslims," know that the equating is not necessary; rather there is a difference between them, and jurisprudence is nobler than medicine in three respects.
The first is that it is a knowledge of the Sacred Law, since it is derived from prophethood, unlike medicine, which is not part of the knowledge of the Law.
The second is that none of those who travel the path of the Hereafter can do without it at all, neither the healthy nor the sick.
As for medicine, only the sick need it, and they are the minority.

The third is that the knowledge of jurisprudence is adjacent to the knowledge of the path of the Hereafter, because it looks into the actions of the limbs, and the source and origin of the actions of the limbs are the qualities of hearts. So praiseworthy actions issue from praiseworthy character traits that bring salvation in the Hereafter, and blameworthy actions issue from blameworthy ones. The connection of the limbs with the heart is not hidden.

As for health and sickness, their origin is clarity in the temperament and the humours, and that belongs to the attributes of the body, not the attributes of the heart. So when jurisprudence is set beside medicine, its nobility appears; and when the knowledge of the path of the Hereafter is set beside jurisprudence, the nobility of the knowledge of the path of the Hereafter appears as well.
If you say, "Then explain to me the knowledge of the path of the Hereafter in detail, in a way that points to its chapter headings, even if it is not possible to exhaust its details,"

know that it is of two kinds: the knowledge of unveiling ('ilm al-mukashafa) and the knowledge of conduct ('ilm al-mu'amala). The first kind is the knowledge of unveiling, which is the knowledge of the inward, and that is the utmost of the sciences. One of the knowers of Allah ('arifin) said, "Whoever has no share of this knowledge, I fear for him an evil end." The least share of it is to affirm it and to yield it to its people.

Another said, "Whoever has two traits will have nothing of this knowledge opened to him: innovation or arrogance." And it was said that whoever is a lover of this world or persists in caprice does not attain realization of it, though he may attain realization of the other sciences. The lightest punishment of whoever denies it is that he tastes nothing of it. A verse is recited in agreement with his statement:

Be content with the absence of whoever is absent from you,
for that is a sin whose punishment lies within it.

It is the knowledge of the truthful ones (siddiqin) and of those brought near (muqarrabun), I mean the knowledge of unveiling. It is an expression for a light that appears in the heart when it is purified and cleansed of its

blameworthy qualities. Through that light many things are unveiled, whose names he used to hear beforehand and for which he imagined vague meanings that were not clear; they then become clear, until true knowledge is attained of the Essence of Allah, glorified is He, and of His enduring, perfect attributes, and of His acts, and of His wisdom in creating this world and the Hereafter, and the reason for His making the Hereafter dependent on this world; and knowledge of the meaning of prophethood and the prophet, the meaning of revelation, the meaning of Satan, the meaning of the words "angels" and "devils," how the devils show enmity toward man, how the angel appears to the prophets, and how revelation reaches them; and knowledge of the dominion of the heavens and the earth; knowledge of the heart and how the armies of the angels and the devils clash within it; knowledge of the difference between the prompting of the angel and the prompting of Satan; and knowledge of the Hereafter, Paradise, the Fire, the punishment of the grave, the Bridge (sirat), the Scale (mizan), and the reckoning; the meaning of His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 17:14⟧ and the meaning of His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 29:64⟧; the meaning of meeting Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and looking upon His noble face; the meaning of nearness to Him and of dwelling beside Him; the meaning of attaining happiness through the company of the highest assembly and the companionship of the angels and the prophets; the meaning of the differing degrees of the people of the gardens, such that some of them see others as one sees the pearl-like star in the middle of the sky; and other things besides, whose detail would be long. For people, concerning the meanings of these matters after affirming their foundations, have various stations. Some think that all of that is symbolic, and that what Allah has prepared for His righteous servants is what no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being, and that creation has of Paradise only attributes and names.

Others think that some of these are symbolic, while some correspond to their realities as understood from their wording. Likewise, some think that the utmost of knowing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is to acknowledge the inability to know Him; some claim great things about knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; and some say that the limit of knowing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is what the belief of all the common people reaches, namely that He is existent, knowing, powerful, hearing, seeing, and speaking. By the knowledge of unveiling we mean that the veil is lifted so that the clear truth in these matters becomes plain to him, with a plainness that is like direct sight about which there is no doubt. This is possible in the essence of man, were it not that the mirror of the heart has had its rust and filth piled up by the dirt of this world. What we mean by the knowledge of the path of the Hereafter is only the knowledge of how to polish this mirror of these impurities, which are the veil from Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and from knowledge of His attributes and acts. Its clearing and cleansing is only by restraining from appetites and by following the prophets (blessings and peace of Allah be upon them) in all their states. To the extent that the heart is cleared and made to face the direction of the Truth, its realities shine in it. There is no way to this except by spiritual discipline (riyada), whose detail will come in its place, and by knowledge and teaching. These are the sciences that are not written down in books and that one whom Allah has favoured with something of them speaks of only with its people, and he is a partner in it by way of mutual discussion and in the manner of secrets. This is the hidden knowledge that he (peace and blessings be upon him) meant by his saying, "Indeed, among knowledge is something like a concealed thing, which none knows except the people who know Allah Most High. When they speak of it, none is ignorant of it except those deluded about Allah Most High. So do not belittle a scholar to whom Allah Most High has given knowledge from Himself, for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not belittle him when He gave it to him." (١) As for the second kind, the knowledge of conduct, it is the knowledge of the states of the heart. As for what is praised among them, it is such things as patience, gratitude, fear, hope, contentment, renunciation, God-consciousness, contentment with little, generosity, knowing Allah Most High's favour in all states, doing good, thinking well, good character, good companionship, truthfulness, and sincerity. So knowing the realities of these states, their definitions, the causes by which they are acquired, their fruit, their sign, and treating what has grown weak among them until it becomes strong, and what has gone until it returns, is part of the knowledge of the Hereafter.

As for what is blameworthy, it is fear of poverty, discontent with what is decreed, malice, rancour, envy, deceit, seeking eminence, love of praise, love of a long stay in this world for the sake of enjoyment, arrogance, showing off (riya'), anger, haughtiness, enmity, hatred, greed, miserliness, craving, extravagance, exuberance, insolence, honouring the rich, belittling the poor, boasting, conceit, rivalry, vainglory, refusing the truth out of arrogance, engaging in what does not concern one, love of much talk, bragging, adorning oneself for people, flattery, self-admiration ('ujb), being occupied with the faults of people instead of one's own faults, the disappearance of sorrow from the heart and the departure of awe from it, intense defence of oneself when humiliation befalls it, weak defence of the truth, taking brothers in public while harbouring enmity in secret, feeling secure from the scheme of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in taking away what He has given, relying on obedience, scheming, betrayal, deception, long hope, hardness, harshness, rejoicing in this world and grief at its loss, intimacy with creatures and desolation at parting from them, coarseness, rashness, haste, scant modesty, and scant mercy. These and their like, among the qualities of the heart, are the planting grounds of indecencies and the soil of forbidden deeds.

and their opposites, which are the praiseworthy character traits, the source of acts of obedience and of nearness. So the knowledge of the limits of these matters, their realities, their causes, their fruits, and their treatment is the knowledge of the Hereafter, and it is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) according to the ruling of the scholars of the Hereafter. Whoever turns away from it is destroyed by the might of the King of kings in the Hereafter, just as whoever turns away from outward actions is destroyed by the sword of the sultans of this world, by the ruling of the jurists of this world. So the jurists' concern with individual obligations relates to the good order of this world, while this relates to the good order of the Hereafter. If a jurist were asked about one of these meanings, even about sincerity, for example, or reliance on Allah, or the way to guard against showing off, he would hesitate over it, although it is his individual obligation, whose neglect is his ruin in the Hereafter. Yet if you asked him about li'an and zihar and racing and archery, he would recite to you volumes of subtle ramifications over which ages would pass, none of which he needs; and if any of it were needed, the town would not lack someone to handle it and spare him the toil of it. Still he keeps toiling over them night and day, and in memorising and studying them he neglects what is important for himself in religion. When he is consulted about it, he says, "I busied myself with it because it is the knowledge of religion and a communal obligation (fard kifaya)," and he misleads himself and others in learning it. The discerning one knows that if his aim were to fulfil the right of the command in the communal obligation, he would put the individual obligation before it; indeed, he would put before it many communal obligations. How many a town has no physician except one of the ahl adh-dhimma, whose testimony cannot be accepted in the rulings of jurisprudence that concern physicians! Yet we see no one busying himself with it, while they contend over the knowledge of jurisprudence, especially disputes and dialectics, though the town is crowded with jurists, those who busy themselves with giving rulings and answering cases. Would that I knew how the jurists of religion allow busying oneself with a communal obligation already fulfilled by a group while neglecting what no one fulfils! Is there any reason for this other than that medicine does not make it easy to reach, through it, the administration of endowments and bequests, the taking possession of the property of orphans, the assumption of judgeship and authority, preeminence over peers, and domination over enemies? Far from it, far from it! The knowledge of religion has been effaced through the deception of the wicked scholars. Allah Most High is the One whose help is sought, and to Him is the refuge, that He protect us from this delusion that angers the Merciful and makes Satan laugh. The scrupulous among the scholars of the outward used to acknowledge the excellence of the scholars of the inward and the masters of hearts. Imam ash-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) used to sit before Shayban the shepherd as a boy sits in school, and ask him how to act in such and such a case. It was said to him, "A man like you asks this Bedouin?" He would say, "This man has been granted success in what we neglected."

Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah be pleased with him) and Yahya ibn Ma'in used to frequent Ma'ruf al-Karkhi, though he was not in the knowledge of the outward of their rank, and they used to ask him. How could it be otherwise, when the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), on being asked, "What should we do if a matter comes to us that we do not find in a book or in the Sunna?", said, "Ask the righteous, and make it a matter of consultation among them"

(١) For this reason it was said, "The scholars of the outward are the adornment of the earth and the kingdom (mulk), and the scholars of the inward are the adornment of the heaven and the realm of dominion (malakut)."

Al-Junayd (may Allah have mercy on him) said: One day as-Sari, my shaykh, said to me, "When you get up from my place, whom do you sit with?" I said, "Al-Muhasibi." He said, "Yes. Take from his knowledge and draw him near, and leave aside his elaborate hair-splitting in discourse and his refutation of the theologians (mutakallimun)." Then, when I turned away, I heard him say, "May Allah make you a master of hadith who is a Sufi, and not make you a Sufi who is a master of hadith." He was pointing out that whoever acquires hadith and knowledge and then takes up Sufism succeeds, and whoever takes up Sufism before knowledge puts himself at risk.

If you say, "Why did you not include theology (kalam) and philosophy among the divisions of the sciences and explain whether the two are blameworthy or praiseworthy?", know that the sum of what theology contains of useful proofs is contained in the Qur'an and the reports. What goes beyond them is either blameworthy disputation, which is among the innovations, as its explanation will come; or quibbling, by clinging to the contradictions the sects raise against it, and lengthening by relating opinions, most of which are absurdities and ravings that natures despise and ears spit out, some of which are delving into what has no bearing on religion. None of it was familiar in the first age, and delving into it altogether was among the innovations. But its ruling has now changed, since an innovation has arisen that turns people away from what the Qur'an and the Sunna require, and a group has emerged who devised doubts for it and arranged composed discourse about it. So that prohibited thing became permitted by necessity; indeed it became a communal obligation, and it is the amount with which the innovator is confronted when he sets out to call to innovation, up to a defined limit that we will mention in the chapter that follows this one, if Allah Most High wills. As for philosophy, it is not a science on its own; rather, it is four parts.

The first is geometry and arithmetic, and the two are permissible, as has preceded, and no one is barred from them except someone for whom it is feared that he will pass through them to blameworthy sciences, since most of those who practise them have gone from them into innovations. So the weak person is kept away from them, not for their own sake, just as a child is kept away from the bank of a river for fear that he will fall into the river, and as one recently come to Islam is kept from mixing with unbelievers for fear for him, although the strong one is not encouraged to mix with them.
The second is logic, which is an inquiry into the aspect of proof and its conditions and the aspect of definition and its conditions, and the two are included in theology.

The third is divine matters (ilahiyyat), which is an inquiry into the Essence of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and His attributes; it too is included in theology. The philosophers did not stand apart in it with another kind of knowledge; rather, they stood apart with doctrines, some of which are unbelief and some innovation. Just as Mu'tazilism is not a science on its own, but its adherents are a group of the theologians, people of inquiry and reasoning, who stood apart with false doctrines, so too are the philosophers.

The fourth is the natural sciences. Some of them contradict the Law, the religion, and the truth; that is ignorance and not knowledge, so it is not something we should list among the divisions of the sciences. And some of them are an inquiry into the attributes of bodies, their properties, and how they transform and change, and this resembles the inquiry of physicians, except that the physician looks specifically at the human body in respect of how it falls sick and becomes healthy, while they look at all bodies in respect of how they change and move. But medicine has an excellence over it, which is that it is needed.

As for their natural sciences, there is no need of them. So theology has become one of the crafts that are obligatory as a communal obligation, to guard the hearts of the common people against the fancies of the innovators. This arose only with the arising of innovations, just as man's need to hire an escort (badhraqa) on the pilgrimage road arose with the arising of the wrongdoing of the Arabs and their highway robbery. Had the Arabs abandoned their aggression, hiring guards would not have been among the conditions of the pilgrimage road. Likewise, had the innovator abandoned his ravings, there would be no need for anything beyond what was known in the age of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). So the theologian should know his limit in religion, and that his place in it is the place of the guard on the pilgrimage road. When the guard devotes himself solely to guarding, he is not among the pilgrims; and the theologian, when he devotes himself solely to debate and defence, and has not travelled the path of the Hereafter, and has not busied himself with tending

the heart and its soundness, is not at all among the scholars of religion. The theologian has of religion only the creed that the rest of the common people share with him, which is among the actions of the outward of the heart and the tongue; he is distinguished from the layman only by the craft of disputation and guarding. As for knowledge of Allah Most High, His attributes and acts, and all that we have pointed to in the knowledge of unveiling, it does not come from theology; indeed, theology almost becomes a veil over it and an obstacle to it. Reaching it is only through spiritual struggle (mujahada), which Allah, glorified is He, made a preliminary to guidance when He said, Most High, ⟦QS 29:69⟧

If you say, "You have reduced the limit of the theologian to guarding the creed of the common people against the disturbance of the innovators, just as the limit of the escort is guarding the pilgrims' goods against the plunder of the Arabs, and you have reduced the limit of the jurist to preserving the law by which the sultan restrains the evil of some wrongdoers from others; and these are two lowly ranks relative to the knowledge of religion. Yet the scholars of the community famed for excellence are the jurists and the theologians, and they are the best of creation in the sight of Allah Most High. So how can you lower their degrees to this base station relative to the knowledge of religion?" know that whoever knows the truth through men is bewildered in the wildernesses of error. Know the truth and you will know its people, if you are travelling the path of truth. And if you are content with imitation and with looking at what is famed of degrees of excellence among people, then do not neglect the Companions and the loftiness of their rank. For those you alluded to are agreed on the precedence of the Companions, and that their stature in religion cannot be reached and their dust cannot be overtaken. Their precedence was not through theology and jurisprudence, but through the knowledge of the Hereafter and travelling its path. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) did not excel people through much fasting, nor through prayer, nor through much narration, nor through giving rulings, nor through theology, but through something that settled in his chest (١), as the master of the messengers (peace and blessings be upon him) testified for him. So let your eagerness be in seeking that secret, for it is the precious jewel and the hidden pearl, and leave aside what most people agree upon, and on magnifying and exalting it, for reasons and motives that would take long to detail. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) passed away leaving thousands of Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), all of them knowers of Allah, whom the Messenger of Allah praised, and among them none was skilled in the craft of theology, and none of them set himself up to give rulings except ten-odd men. Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) was among them, and when he was asked for a ruling he would say to the asker, "Go to so-and-so the commander, who has taken on the affairs of the people and put them around his neck," pointing to the fact that giving rulings in cases and judgments is among the appendages of authority and sultanate. When 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) died, Ibn Mas'ud said, "Nine-tenths of knowledge has died." It was said to him, "Do you say that when the great Companions are among us?" He said, "I did not mean the knowledge of rulings and judgments; I mean only the knowledge of Allah Most High." Do you think he meant the craft of theology and dialectic? Then why are you not eager to know that knowledge, nine-tenths of which died with the death of 'Umar? He is the one who shut the door of theology and dialectic, who struck Dabi' with the whip when he brought him a question about the conflict of two verses in the Book of Allah, and who boycotted him and ordered the people to boycott him. As for your saying that the famed among the scholars are the jurists and the theologians, know that what one attains excellence with in the sight of Allah is one thing and what one attains fame with among people is another. The fame of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) was through the caliphate, and his excellence through the secret that settled in his heart. The fame of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) was through governance, and his excellence through the knowledge of Allah, nine-tenths of which died with his death, and through his aim of drawing near to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in his rule, his justice, and his compassion for His creation, which is an inward matter in his secret. As for all his other outward actions, their issuing from one who seeks status, name, and reputation, and who desires fame, can be imagined. So fame lies in what is ruinous, and excellence in what is a secret that no one is aware of. The jurists and the theologians are like the caliphs, the judges, and the scholars, and they have divided: among them are those who wanted Allah, glorified is He, by their knowledge, their rulings, and their defence of

the Sunna of His Prophet, and did not seek by it showing off or reputation. Those are the people of the good pleasure of Allah Most High, and their excellence in the sight of Allah is for their acting on their knowledge and for their seeking the face of Allah, glorified is He, by their rulings and their inquiry. For all knowledge is action, since it is an acquired act, but not every action is knowledge. The physician can draw near to Allah Most High by his knowledge, so he is rewarded for his knowledge in that he acts for Allah, glorified and exalted is He, by it; and the sultan mediates between creatures for Allah's sake, so he is pleasing to Allah, glorified is He, and rewarded, not in that he is responsible for the knowledge of religion, but in that he holds a task by which he intends to draw near to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by his knowledge.

The kinds of what one draws near to Allah Most High by are three: pure knowledge, which is the knowledge of unveiling; pure action, such as the justice of the sultan, for example, and his control over people; and a compound of action and knowledge, which is the knowledge of the path of the Hereafter, for its possessor is of the scholars and the doers together. So look to yourself: will you be on the Day of the Resurrection in the party of the scholars of Allah, or of those who act for Allah Most High, or in both parties, so that you take your share with each of the two groups? This is more important for you than imitation for the sake of mere fame, as it was said:

Take what you see and leave what you have only heard of;
in the rising of the sun is what spares you Saturn.

Moreover, we shall relate from the conduct of the jurists of the early generations (salaf) what will let you know that those who claimed their schools wronged them, and that they will be among their fiercest adversaries on the Day of the Resurrection, for they sought by knowledge only the face of Allah Most High. Of their states there was witnessed what is among the signs of the scholars of the Hereafter, as its explanation will come in the chapter on the signs of the scholars of the Hereafter. They were not devoted solely to the knowledge of jurisprudence; rather they were occupied with the knowledge of hearts and observing them. But what turned them from teaching and authoring in it is what turned the Companions from authoring and teaching in jurisprudence, although they were independent jurists in the knowledge of giving rulings. The diverting factors and motives are certain, and there is no need to mention them.

Now we shall mention of the states of the jurists of Islam what will let you know that what we have said is not an attack on them, but an attack on those who display emulating them while claiming their schools, yet contradict them in their actions and conduct. The jurists who are the leaders of jurisprudence and the guides of the people, I mean those with many followers among the schools, are five: ash-Shafi'i, Malik, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Hanifa, and Sufyan ath-Thawri (may Allah Most High have mercy on them).

Each of them was a worshipper, a renunciant, a knower of the sciences of the Hereafter, a jurist in the interests of creation in this world, and one who sought by his jurisprudence the face of Allah Most High. These are five traits. The jurists of the age have followed them in only one of them, which is exerting oneself and going to extremes in the ramifications of jurisprudence, because the four traits are fit only for the Hereafter, whereas this one trait is fit for this world and the Hereafter; if the Hereafter is intended by it, its fitness for this world is reduced. They have exerted themselves for it and claim by it resemblance to those imams. Far from it that angels be measured against blacksmiths! So let us now relate of their states what indicates these four traits, for their knowledge of jurisprudence is evident.

As for Imam ash-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him), what indicates that he was a worshipper is what is related, that he used to divide the night into three parts: a third for knowledge, a third for worship, and a third for sleep. Ar-Rabi' said, "Ash-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) used to complete the Qur'an in Ramadan sixty times, all of that in prayer." Al-Buwayti, one of his companions, used to complete the Qur'an in Ramadan once every day. Al-Hasan al-Karabisi said, "I spent more than one night with ash-Shafi'i. He would pray about a third of the night, and I never saw him exceed fifty verses; if he did more, then a hundred verses. He never passed a verse of mercy without asking Allah for himself and for all Muslims and believers, and never passed a verse of punishment without seeking refuge in Allah from it and asking deliverance for himself and for the believers. It was as though hope and fear had been gathered for him together." So see how his limiting himself to fifty verses indicates his depth in the secrets of the Qur'an and his reflection on them. Ash-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said, "I have not eaten my fill for sixteen years, because fullness weighs down the body, hardens the heart, removes sharpness of mind, brings sleep, and weakens its owner for worship." So see his wisdom in mentioning the harms of fullness, then his earnestness in worship, in that he cast fullness aside for its sake, for the head of devotion is reducing food. Ash-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said, "I have never sworn by Allah Most High, neither truthfully nor falsely." So see
his reverence and veneration for Allah Most High, and how that indicates his knowledge of the majesty of Allah, glorified is He.

Ash-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about a question and was silent. It was said to him, "Will you not answer, may Allah have mercy on you?" He said, "Until I know whether the excellence lies in my silence or in my answer." So see his watchfulness over his tongue, though it is the limb with the most power over jurists and the most disobedient to control and subjugation. By this it becomes clear that he never spoke and never kept silent except to attain excellence and seek reward.

Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn al-Wazir said, "Ash-Shafi'i (may Allah Most High have mercy on him) went out one day from the lamp market and we followed him. There was a man abusing a man of knowledge. Ash-Shafi'i turned to us and said, 'Keep your ears clean of listening to obscenity, as you keep your tongues clean of uttering it. The listener is a partner of the speaker, and the foul-mouthed looks at the filthiest thing in his vessel and is eager to pour it into your vessels. If the word of the foul-mouthed were rejected, whoever rejected it would be happy, just as the one who said it is wretched through it.'"

Ash-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "A sage wrote to another sage, 'You have been given knowledge, so do not stain your knowledge with the darkness of sins, lest you remain in darkness on the day when the people of knowledge hasten by the light of their knowledge.'"

As for his renunciation (may Allah be pleased with him), ash-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) said, "Whoever claims that he has combined in his heart the love of this world and the love of its Creator has lied."

Al-Humaydi said, "Ash-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) went out to Yemen with one of the governors and returned to Mecca with ten thousand dirhams. A tent was pitched for him in a place outside Mecca, and people kept coming to him, and he did not leave that place until he had distributed all of it. Once he came out of the bath and gave the bath attendant a large sum of money. Once his whip fell from his hand and someone picked it up and handed it to him, and he gave him fifty dinars in return for it."
